newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rain hits Australia landslide site, death toll up.
newsitem.headline: Rain hits Australia landslide site, death toll up.

text.p: Rescuers on Wednesday pulled a 13th body from the rubble of a week-old landslide at an Australian ski village as rain forced them to speed up their search against the odds for more survivors.

Light rain and gusts of wind swept the scarred mountainside at Thredbo village, in the Snowy Mountains south of Sydney, breaking a spell of fine weather which was crucial to the miraculous survival of ski instructor Stuart Diver.
Diver was unearthed from his concrete tomb deep within the debris on Saturday, three freezing nights after the hillside gave way, engulfing two ski lodges and burying 19 people.
Shrouded in blue plastic, a dead woman was pulled from a crack in the same pile of concrete slabs on Wednesday morning and taken by stretcher up the treacherous slope as patchy rain fell.
Five people are still missing among the broken concrete slabs in what police believe are the crushed remains of some bedrooms near where Diver was found alive.
Diver was in bed with his wife, Sally, when disaster struck.
So far, the bodies of eight men and five women have been recovered. Police said on Wednesday they would not identify any of them until all the missing people were accounted for.
But rescuers continue to hope against grim odds for another miracle.
"We are hopeful that perhaps there is a glimmer of light there...," police superintendent Paul Chaplin said. "We have not counted out the prospect of finding people alive."

Rescuers on Wednesday accelerated the search effort, heeding a forecast of rain and then snow from Wednesday night. They say that if the weather closes in, temperatures will plunge lower and the conditions could disrupt work on the site.
"Speed is going to be the key factor, however we are paramount about the safety of our rescuers...," Chaplin said.
"The magnitude of the weather is such that it's going to pose a great problem to the rescuers," he added.
Ambulance officers at the scene are concerned about rescuers falling prey to hypothermia and plan to replace crews hourly if the weather turns nasty.
If left uncovered in the rain, the hillside could give way again and flood the honeycomb of tunnels painstakingly dug by hand into the rubble in search of cavities that might hide life.
